title: Free Space Management
summary: How a file system tracks which blocks are available for allocation — bitmaps, free lists, and the optimizations that make allocation fast at scale.

slides.markdown:
Every allocation covered in [File Allocation Methods](file-allocation-methods) assumed the file system already knows which blocks are free. Something has to track that, updated on every create, grow, and delete, without itself becoming a bottleneck.

The two classic answers are a **bitmap** (one bit per block, allocated or free) and a **linked free list** (free blocks chained together, exactly like linked file allocation but for empty space). Real file systems mostly use bitmaps with optimizations layered on, which is where this topic ends up.

Allocating a block for a new or growing file requires answering "which blocks are currently unused?" fast — this happens on every write that needs a new block, potentially thousands of times per second on a busy system. The structure also has to survive crashes: if the free-space tracker itself gets corrupted or falls out of sync with reality, the file system can allocate a block that's already in use (silent data corruption) or permanently lose track of a free block (a slow leak of usable space).

The design questions are: how much space does the tracker itself cost, and how fast can it answer "give me a free block" or "give me N contiguous free blocks"?

A **bitmap** dedicates one bit per block: 1 for allocated, 0 for free (or vice versa). For a 1TB disk with 4KB blocks, that's 256 million blocks — a bitmap of 32MB, small enough to load entirely into RAM and keep resident.

Finding a free block means scanning for a 0 bit; finding N *contiguous* free blocks means scanning for a run of N zero bits — both easy operations on a bitmap held in memory, and CPUs have fast bit-manipulation instructions (population count, find-first-set) that make this scan cheap even over megabytes of bitmap.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a block bitmap with allocated/free bits
slides.markdown:
![bitmap free run of blocks](assets/bitmap-free-run.svg)

Each square is one bit, one block. The scan for "find 5 contiguous free blocks" is literally looking for 5 consecutive 0 bits in this row — cheap when the bitmap fits in a CPU cache line or two, since modern CPUs can test many bits per instruction.

The bracket makes the payoff concrete: this exact bitmap segment can satisfy one contiguous 20KB allocation without any fragmentation-avoidance logic beyond "find the run."

A **linked free list** chains every free block to the next free block, exactly mirroring linked file allocation but for unused space — the superblock just needs a pointer to the head of the chain. Allocating a block means popping the head off the list; freeing a block means pushing it back on.

The weakness mirrors linked allocation's weakness: finding N *contiguous* free blocks means walking the list checking adjacency, an O(n) operation with no shortcut, versus a bitmap's near-constant-time bit scan. A pure free list also can't answer "how much free space is left" without walking the entire chain, whereas a bitmap can maintain a running free-block counter trivially.

slides.sectionTitle: Grouping and counting optimizations over a naive free list
slides.markdown:
Two classic fixes make a free list competitive. **Grouping**: instead of one block pointing to the next single block, the first free block in a group stores the addresses of the next *n* free blocks (not just one) — so acquiring n blocks at once is one lookup instead of n chain hops. **Counting**: since free blocks are often allocated and freed in contiguous runs (a file's blocks are usually adjacent), store `(start block, count)` pairs instead of one entry per block — a 100-block free run becomes one list entry instead of 100.

Both optimizations exploit the same real-world pattern: free space tends to be spatially clustered, not uniformly scattered, so representing it in runs rather than singletons shrinks both the metadata size and the lookup cost.

| | Bitmap | Linked free list (with grouping/counting) |
|---|---|---|
| Space overhead | Fixed, small (~1 bit/block regardless of fragmentation) | Grows with fragmentation — worst case, one entry per free block |
| Finding N contiguous blocks | Fast bit-scan, cache-friendly | O(n) walk unless already grouped by luck |
| Total free space query | Maintain a running counter — O(1) | Requires walking the whole structure unless separately tracked |
| Crash recovery | Corruption is localized to specific bits | A broken pointer can silently drop an entire tail of the free list |
| Real-world use | ext4, NTFS (both bitmap-based) | Older/simpler file systems; largely superseded |

**How to decide:** for a general-purpose file system, a bitmap wins on nearly every axis — the only real advantage a free list ever had was avoiding a fixed-size structure sized for the disk's full block count, which stopped mattering once disks got cheap enough that a 32MB bitmap for 1TB is a rounding error.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: bitmap size and scan cost at scale
slides.markdown:
A 4TB drive with 4KB blocks has 1 billion blocks, needing a 125MB bitmap — still small enough to keep cached in RAM on any modern server, though large enough that some file systems split it into per-block-group chunks (ext4's approach) so a small allocation only needs to scan and lock the relevant chunk, not the whole bitmap.

A population-count instruction can test 64 bits (one bitmap word) per CPU cycle in the best case, so scanning even a 125MB bitmap for a free run — worst case, every bit examined — costs low single-digit milliseconds; in practice, allocators keep a cached "last known free region" hint and rarely scan from the start, making real allocation calls microseconds, not milliseconds.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming free space tracking never needs its own consistency guarantees
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Free space bitmaps are just bookkeeping — they can't cause real data loss if something goes wrong."

**Why it's wrong:** if a crash leaves the bitmap out of sync with reality — say, a block was actually allocated to a file but the bitmap update never made it to disk — the allocator can hand that same block to a *second* file. Both files now believe they own it, and whichever writes last silently corrupts the other's data. This is a genuine crash-consistency hazard, not just lost bookkeeping.

**Correct model:** free space metadata needs the same crash-consistency protection as file data and inodes — which is exactly why it's typically covered by the same journal described in [Journaling & Crash Consistency](journaling-and-crash-consistency): a bitmap update and the block allocation it represents are written as one atomic transaction, so a crash mid-way replays cleanly instead of leaving two files sharing one block.
